statement: If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line which is called binomial.
heath_proof: For let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the first binomial AD; I say that the “side” of the area AC is the irrational straight line which is called binomial. For, since AD is a first binomial straight line, let it be divided into its terms at E, and let AE be the greater term. It is then manifest that AE, ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE, and AE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB set out. [X. Deff. II. 1] Let ED be bisected at the point F. Then, since the square on AE is greater than the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable with AE, therefore, if there be applied to the greater AE a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less, that is, to the square on EF, and deficient by a square figure, it divides it into commensurable parts. [X. 17] Let then the rectangle AG, GE equal to the square on EF be applied to AE; therefore AG is commensurable in length with EG. Let GH, EK, FL be drawn from G, E, F parallel to either of the straight lines AB, CD; let the square SN be constructed equal to the parallelogram AH, and the square NQ equal to GK, [II. 14] and let them be placed so that MN is in a straight line with NO; therefore RN is also in a straight line with NP. And let the parallelogram SQ be completed; therefore SQ is a square. [Lemma] Now, since the rectangle AG, GE is equal to the square on EF, therefore, as AG is to EF, so is FE to EG; [VI. 17] therefore also, as AH is to EL, so is EL to KG; [VI. 1] therefore EL is a mean proportional between AH, GK. But AH is equal to SN, and GK to NQ; therefore EL is a mean proportional between SN, NQ. But MR is also a mean proportional between the same SN, NQ; [Lemma]therefore EL is equal to MR, so that it is also equal to PO. But AH, GK are also equal to SN, NQ; therefore the whole AC is equal to the whole SQ, that is, to the square on MO; therefore MO is the “side” of AC. I say next that MO is binomial. For, since AG is commensurable with GE, therefore AE is also commensurable with each of the straight lines AG, GE. [X. 15] But AE is also, by hypothesis, commensurable with AB; therefore AG, GE are also commensurable with AB. [X. 12] And AB is rational; therefore each of the straight lines AG, GE is also rational; therefore each of the rectangles AH, GK is rational, [X. 19] and AH is commensurable with GK. But AH is equal to SN, and GK to NQ; therefore SN, NQ, that is, the squares on MN, NO, are rational and commensurable. And, since AE is incommensurable in length with ED, while AE is commensurable with AG, and DE is commensurable with EF, therefore AG is also incommensurable with EF, [X. 13] so that AH is also incommensurable with EL. [VI. 1, X. 11] But AH is equal to SN, and EL to MR; therefore SN is also incommensurable with MR. But, as SN is to MR, so is PN to NR; [VI. 1] therefore PN is incommensurable with NR. [X. 11] But PN is equal to MN, and NR to NO; therefore MN is incommensurable with NO. And the square on MN is commensurable with the square on NO, and each is rational; therefore MN, NO are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Therefore MO is binomial [X. 36] and the “side” of AC.

**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and the first binomial, the âsideâ of the area is the irrational straight line which is called binomial.

**Step 1.** Let the area AC be contained by the rational straight line AB and the first binomial straight line AD. We must show that the "side" of AC (the straight line whose square equals AC) is the irrational straight line called binomial.

**Step 2.** Since AD is a first binomial, let it be divided into its terms at E, with AE the greater term. By D10.2.1, AE and ED are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, the square on AE exceeds the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, and the greater term AE is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AB.

**Step 3.** Bisect ED at F, so that EF equals half of ED. Since the square on AE exceeds the square on ED by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AE, by 10.17, if we apply to AE a rectangle equal to the square on EF and deficient by a square figure, it divides AE into parts commensurable in length. Let G be the point on AE such that the rectangle AG by GE equals the square on EF, with the applied figure deficient by a square. Then AG is commensurable in length with GE.

**Step 4.** Since AG is commensurable in length with GE, by 10.15 the whole AE is also commensurable in length with each of AG and GE. Since AE is commensurable in length with AB (from the definition of the first binomial), by 10.12, both AG and GE are commensurable in length with AB. Hence AB, AG, and GE are all rational straight lines commensurable in length with one another.

**Step 5.** Let p be the straight line such that the square on p equals the rectangle AB by AG, and let q be the straight line such that the square on q equals the rectangle AB by GE. Such lines exist by the converse construction of squares equal to given rectangles.

**Step 6.** Since AB and AG are rational and commensurable in length, the rectangle AB by AG is rational, by 10.19. Likewise, since AB and GE are rational and commensurable in length, the rectangle AB by GE is rational, by 10.19. Therefore the squares on p and on q are each rational areas, so p and q are each rational straight lines, by D10.1.4.

**Step 7.** Now consider the sum of the squares on p and q. We have the square on p plus the square on q equals (AB times AG) plus (AB times GE) equals AB times (AG + GE), by 2.1. Since AG + GE = AE, this equals AB times AE. Since AE is commensurable in length with AB and both are rational, the rectangle AB by AE is rational, by 10.19. Therefore the sum of the squares on p and q is rational.

**Step 8.** Since AG is commensurable in length with GE, the ratio AG to GE is a ratio of number to number, by 10.5. Therefore the rectangle AB by AG has to the rectangle AB by GE the same ratio (since the common side AB cancels), and so the square on p is to the square on q as AG is to GE, which is a ratio commensurable magnitudes have. By 10.6, the square on p is commensurable with the square on q. Thus p and q are commensurable in square, by D10.1.2.

**Step 9.** We now show that p and q are incommensurable in length. Consider twice the rectangle contained by p and q. By the relation between the rectangle under two lines and the geometric mean, the square on the rectangle p by q equals (the square on p) times (the square on q) = (AB times AG) times (AB times GE) = the square on AB times the rectangle AG by GE. Since the rectangle AG by GE equals the square on EF (Step 3), we get that the square of the rectangle p by q equals the square on AB times the square on EF. Therefore the rectangle p by q equals AB times EF, by 6.17.

**Step 10.** Thus twice the rectangle p by q equals 2 times (AB times EF) = AB times (2 times EF) = AB times ED, since EF is half of ED.

**Step 11.** Now AE is commensurable in length with AB, and AE is commensurable in square only with ED (by the definition of the first binomial). If ED were commensurable in length with AB, then by 10.12, ED would be commensurable in length with AE, contradicting that AE and ED are commensurable in square only. Therefore ED is incommensurable in length with AB, by 10.13.

**Step 12.** Since AB and ED are each rational but commensurable in square only (Step 11 and D10.1.3), the rectangle AB by ED is irrational, by 10.21. Therefore twice the rectangle p by q, which equals AB times ED, is irrational.

**Step 13.** Since the sum of the squares on p and q is rational (Step 7) and twice the rectangle p by q is irrational (Step 12), these two areas are incommensurable (a rational area cannot be commensurable with an irrational area). Therefore p and q are incommensurable in square with respect to the combined expression, which means p and q cannot be commensurable in length. For if p and q were commensurable in length, then by 10.19, twice the rectangle p by q would be rational (since p and q would be rational lines commensurable in length), contradicting Step 12. Therefore p and q are commensurable in square only.

**Step 14.** Since p and q are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, by 10.36, the sum p + q is the irrational straight line called binomial.

**Step 15.** It remains to show that p + q is the "side" of the area AC. The square on (p + q) equals the square on p plus the square on q plus twice the rectangle p by q, by 2.4. This equals AB times AE plus AB times ED (from Steps 7 and 10). By 2.1, AB times AE plus AB times ED equals AB times (AE + ED) = AB times AD, which is the area AC. Therefore the square on (p + q) equals AC, so p + q is the "side" of the area AC.

**Step 16.** Therefore the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AB and the first binomial straight line AD is the binomial straight line. Q.E.D.
